A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepRUOT work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching theory and experiments relocated in v2.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original synthetic gene-network experiments, including inferred trajectories, growth rates and developmental landscapes in Figures 6.1–6.4.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices B–C report original synthetic and real-data experiments, quantitative baseline comparisons, ablations and sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The three-network solver and its principal losses remain. However, v1 specifies a CFM-only score warmup, whereas v2 Appendix C.3 augments that objective with a temporary penalty on positive log-density-network outputs before removing it. This is a limited revision to the stated training objective.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic gene-network task, v2 adds Gaussian-mixture transport, mouse hematopoiesis and A549 epithelial–mesenchymal transition data. These extend evaluation to substantially different distributions and real biological populations (Section 6; Appendices B.2–B.4).

E2.justification: v1's reported baseline comparison centers on SF2M. v2 Table 1 retains SF2M and adds MIOFlow, unbalanced Action Matching, Unbalanced SB/UDSB and an Unbalanced OT implementation. Table 2 evaluates the expanded comparator set on hematopoiesis.

E3.justification: v2 introduces quantitative W1/W2 evaluation after fitting observed time points, using weighted distributions for DeepRUOT and uniform weights for comparators (Appendix C.1). Its quantitative gene comparison uses diffusion 0.05 for DeepRUOT versus 0.25 for SF2M, separately from the retained 0.25 visual comparison. Added experiments also introduce SPRING/PCA preprocessing and 10–100-dimensional mixture settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled ablations of growth, local mass matching, Fokker–Planck constraints and training stages (Table 4), plus epoch-scheduling and loss-weight sensitivity studies (Tables 6–7). Figures 4 and 7 additionally examine UDSB trajectory and population-mass errors, extending substantially beyond v1's qualitative SF2M comparison.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 1, 2 and 4 explicitly report means and one standard deviation across five runs. v1 provides neither repeated-run counts nor uncertainty summaries. This establishes new statistical reporting, without establishing an increase from any known earlier run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds quantitative comparisons, ablation and sensitivity scores, and mixture/real-data findings. Table 1 reports final gene-data W2 of 0.121 for DeepRUOT versus 0.124 for Unbalanced OT. Superiority is not universal: Table 2's final W1 favors Unbalanced SB, 0.128254 versus 0.132411. These are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Most theorems, proofs and Schrödinger-bridge connections are retained and relocated. A local mathematical revision occurs in Appendix D.2: the entropy endpoint difference gains a sigma-squared factor absent from v1 Section 3.1. The central theoretical framework remains unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion extend the claimed demonstrated applicability from a synthetic gene network to high-dimensional mixtures and real single-cell dynamics. The central contributions—learning RUOT without growth priors, avoiding false transitions and reconstructing landscapes—remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation beyond v1's false-transition and landscape explanations. It discusses growth-versus-transport ambiguity and temporal resolution, scalability difficulties at thousands of dimensions, numerical instability, and mechanisms behind training-stage failures (Section 6; Appendices B–C). The earlier unresolved microscopic Schrödinger-bridge interpretations remain in Appendix E.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, simulation parameters, an explicit initial-density estimator, dataset preprocessing, hardware specifications, loss weights, training schedules and epoch counts (Appendices A–C; Tables 3 and 5). These substantially expand v1's algorithm and library descriptions; newly disclosed settings do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including Maddu et al. (2024), Meng et al. (2024), Weinreb et al. (2020) and Zhang et al. (2021). Section 4 also explicitly contrasts its Fisher cross-term with Baradat and Lavenant's formulation. The broader research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: v2 extensively reorganizes the narrative: it rewrites and condenses the introduction, adds explicit contribution bullets and a separate related-work section, consolidates algorithm presentation, and moves substantial theory and training material into Appendices A–E. This exceeds routine language editing.

P2.justification: v2 combines v1 Figures 6.1–6.4 into a redesigned eight-panel Figure 2, revises the overview diagram, and adds six result figures and seven tables. The ICLR layout and redistributed scientific displays substantially change visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 relies on a qualitative comparison in one simulated system with sparse reproducibility information. v2 substantially addresses these weaknesses through quantitative baseline comparisons, five-run uncertainty reporting, component ablations, sensitivity tests, real-data applications and implementation details. Evaluation on fitted time points, unequal comparator settings and the overstated blanket superiority claim in light of Table 2 limit the conclusions, but the gains in evidence and reproducibility are substantial.
